title: How we got rich by 26: our recession-proof money rules
summary: A personal finance 101 episode in which Cherie and Jean, self-made millionaires in their 20s without family money, explain how choosing a major and first job for earning power created their financial freedom, then walk through beginner (401k matching), intermediate (Ramit Sethi's budgeting framework and money mindset) and advanced (backdoor Roth, HSA, exchange funds, zero-cost collars for concentrated stock) tactics. Key takeaways: information is power, there is no silver bullet beyond compounding good habits, and you do not need to come from money to build wealth, just knowledge, discipline and an understanding of trade-offs.

ideas.idea: The single biggest contributor to becoming a self-made millionaire in your 20s is the first job out of college, which traces back to what you choose to study.
ideas.detail: Jean studied economics at a liberal arts school, noticed which seniors were celebrated for landing McKinsey, Goldman and Morgan Stanley jobs, set a four-year goal of getting into Goldman Sachs, and worked backwards to a junior-year internship and a valuable sophomore-year role.

ideas.idea: It is legitimate to copy the paths of people you admire: be curious, ask questions, gather information, then build a plan you can pivot when reality hits.
ideas.detail: Jean's Goldman internship plan was derailed by the Great Recession, but having a target let her adjust; today the equivalent legwork is Google, Glassdoor, LinkedIn salary data and networking, but you still have to piece together how to get there.

ideas.idea: Choose a major that maximizes your options and earning potential out of school if you have student loans and no family money to fall back on.
ideas.detail: Cherie wanted to be a doctor but Jean, having found it nearly impossible to become a product manager without a CS degree after Goldman, told her in 2013 to study computer science; Cherie admits she could not have pulled off the art-history-to-McKinsey route others did and needed a more bulletproof plan.

ideas.idea: Maximizing earnings early buys freedom later: decisions Cherie made at 19 let her run a podcast and a bootstrapped startup full-time at 29 without venture or angel money.
ideas.detail: The hosts stress this is only one option; if you have no loans and want to explore, that is fine, but be conscious about whether earning potential is what you want to optimize for. Jean notes the CS-degree advice may not hold word for word in 2025 with ChatGPT replacing engineers; the mindset of positioning yourself for your goals is what transfers.

ideas.idea: 401(k) matching is free money that most new grads leave on the table because retirement feels 40 years away.
ideas.detail: Configure it once in the payroll portal and contributions come out automatically every two weeks; Cherie's company matched dollar for dollar, and many match up to a percentage such as 3%. Both hosts maxed out the match.

ideas.idea: 401(k) contributions are pre-tax, so roughly 30% more money goes in to compound for decades and you are taxed only on withdrawal, usually at a lower post-retirement rate.
ideas.detail: Jean's example: $100,000 contributed pre-tax all goes to investments, versus paying about $30,000 in taxes if received as income; the hosts cite roughly 10% average annual growth and stress the power of compounding over 40 years.

ideas.idea: Whether you front-load or drip your 401(k) contributions depends on your need for liquidity; money taken out before you see your paycheck is money you do not miss.
ideas.detail: Cherie's ex-boyfriend maxed out contributions in a short window so his take-home was about $1,000 a month to 'get it over with,' while Cherie spread contributions across the year to avoid seeing a $700 paycheck.

ideas.idea: Ramit Sethi's I Will Teach You to Be Rich changed both sisters' financial lives because it gives directive, specific actions rather than vague advice.
ideas.detail: The book told Jean 15 years ago to open a Charles Schwab checking account online for its ATM-fee refunds and to put money in specific Vanguard funds; those remain her standards today. The hosts note it is really about healthy habits that compound into wealth.
names_or_cases: I Will Teach You to Be Rich

ideas.idea: There is no silver bullet to getting rich; wealth is built by small actions accruing over a long period.
ideas.detail: The hosts did not get rich overnight; everything they did was compounding good financial habits and having a strong foundation after graduation.

ideas.idea: A college scarcity mindset carried into a high-paying first job creates fear-driven paralysis around money, and the cure is running the numbers once.
ideas.detail: Cherie was paralyzed for about five months after graduating, agonizing over a $30 Uber despite a big salary, and discussed it in therapy; the fix was calculating how much she could spend, save and put into her 401(k). Jean was money-avoidant too but was saved by a lucrative job and 90-hour weeks that left no time to spend.

ideas.idea: Budget guideline: about 50% of take-home to fixed costs, 10% to investments, 5-10% to savings, and 20-25% to guilt-free spending.
ideas.detail: Fixed costs are rent, food, car, utilities and student loans, though the sisters always optimized for cheap housing; investments are 401(k) and index funds; savings cover emergencies, travel or a wedding; guilt-free spending on spa, matcha or nails is the bucket Cherie most needed, from Ramit Sethi's framework.

ideas.idea: Once you check that your natural spending fits the guidelines, you can stop actively budgeting, but do not be so frugal that you forget to enjoy life.
ideas.detail: Jean assessed her situation once or twice and never thought about it again, but regrets not being more permissive with clothes she loved; she and her banker and Facebook roommates furnished their first apartment with an $80 smelly Facebook Marketplace couch and a $10 scratched IKEA table while a friend paid $2,500 for a couch.

ideas.idea: Skipping car ownership and using public transit in San Francisco is a real money saver worth being proud of.
ideas.detail: Cherie took the bus to work every day for all her years in SF (the 38R Rapid from Pacific Heights); Jean took the 22 line from Noe Valley.

ideas.idea: Advanced tools to research once the basics are set: backdoor Roth, mega backdoor Roth and HSA.
ideas.detail: The hosts have used these themselves but only name them as terminology to Google, since they are more complex and situation-dependent.

ideas.idea: Tech employees paid heavily in RSUs end up with dangerously concentrated portfolios and should diversify rather than hold 90%+ of net worth in one stock.
ideas.detail: Cherie learned this from a friend who leads a private wealth management team at Morgan Stanley and wishes she had known 5-6 years earlier; she uses NVIDIA engineers as the archetype.

ideas.idea: An exchange fund lets you pool concentrated shares with others and swap into a diversified portfolio without selling and triggering capital gains taxes.
ideas.detail: Minimums are typically several million dollars, often around $5 million, and you must keep the money in the fund for about seven years; Cherie instead sold and reinvested, paying high short-term gains taxes, and was told exchange funds are not new.

ideas.idea: A zero-cost collar, buying a put and selling a call on a concentrated stock, limits your downside while capping upside, and the call premium pays for the put.
ideas.detail: Most retail investors with options approval can do it, but it requires being in the weeds or working with a financial advisor; the hosts place it in the ultra-advanced category.

ideas.idea: You do not need to come from money to build wealth, but you need knowledge, discipline and an understanding of the trade-offs.
ideas.detail: Closing takeaway, paired with the reminder that money does not buy happiness but it can buy freedom and peace of mind; the hosts are not financial advisors, though Jean passed the Series 7 and 63 fifteen years ago.
